{{short description|Theorem in mathematical statistics}}

The '''Darmois–Skitovich theorem''' is one of the most well-known characterization theorems in [[mathematical statistics]]. It characterizes the [[normal distribution]] (the Gaussian distribution) by the independence of two linear forms of <math>n</math> independent [[random variable]]s. The theorem was proved independently in 1953 by [[Vladimir Pavlovich Skitovich|V. P. Skitovich]]<ref>
V. P. Skitovich. On a property of the normal distribution. Doklady Akademii Nauk SSSR (N.S.), vol. 89 (1953), pp. 217–219.
</ref> and [[Georges Darmois]]<ref>
G. Darmois. Analyse générale des liaisons stochastiques: étude particulière de l'analyse factorielle linéaire. Revue de l'Institut International de Statistique, vol. 21, nos. 1/2 (1953), pp. 2–8. https://www.jstor.org/stable/1401511
</ref>, see also <ref>
A. M. Kagan, Yu. V. Linnik, C. R. Rao. Characterization Problems of Mathematical Statistics. Wiley, New York, 1973. ISBN 9780471454212
</ref>, where some of its generalizations can be found.

== Statement of the theorem ==
Let <math>\xi_j, j = 1, 2, \dots, n</math>, be independent random variables, and 
let <math>\alpha_j, \beta_j</math> be nonzero constants. If the linear forms
<math>L_1 = \alpha_1\xi_1 + \dots + \alpha_n\xi_n</math> and <math>L_2 = \beta_1\xi_1 + \dots + \beta_n\xi_n</math> are independent, then the random variables <math>\xi_j</math> are normally distributed (Gaussian).

The Darmois–Skitovich theorem is a generalization of the [[Kac–Bernstein theorem]], in which the normal distribution is characterized by the independence of the sum and difference of two independent random variables.

A result closely related to the Darmois–Skitovich theorem was proved in 1970 by [[Chris Heyde|C. C. Heyde]], where the Gaussian distribution is characterized by the symmetry of the [[conditional distribution]] of one [[linear form]] of <math>n</math> independent random variables given another<ref>
C. C. Heyde. Characterization of the Normal Law by the Symmetry of a Certain Conditional Distribution. Sankhyā: The Indian Journal of Statistics, Series A, vol. 32, no. 1 (1970), pp. 115–118. https://www.jstor.org/stable/25049642
</ref>.

== Generalizations  to locally compact Abelian groups==
The Darmois–Skitovich theorem has been extended in various directions. In particular, many works are devoted to its generalization to the case where independent random variables take values in a locally compact [[Abelian group]]  and the coefficients of the linear forms are topological automorphisms of the group. A survey of a significant part of these results can be found in <ref>
G. Feldman. Characterization of Probability Distributions on Locally Compact Abelian Groups. Mathematical Surveys and Monographs, vol. 273. American Mathematical Society, Providence, RI, 2023. ISBN 978-1-4704-7295-5
</ref>. A typical example of a group  analogue of the Darmois–Skitovich theorem is the following result.

'''Theorem'''<ref>G.M. Feldman. A characterization of the Gaussian distribution on Abelian groups. Probab. Theory Relat. Fields. Vol. 126, no. 1 (2003),   91–102. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00440-003-0256-4</ref>.  Let <math>X</math> be a second countable locally compact Abelian group containing no subgroups topologically isomorphic to the [[circle group]]. Let <math>\xi_j, j = 1, 2, \dots, n</math>, be independent random variables taking values in <math>X</math> with distributions <math>\mu_j</math> whose characteristic functions do not vanish. Let <math>\alpha_j, \beta_j</math> be topological automorphisms of  <math>X</math>. If the linear forms <math>L_1 = \alpha_1\xi_1 + \dots + \alpha_n\xi_n</math> and <math>L_2 = \beta_1\xi_1 + \dots + \beta_n\xi_n</math> are independent, then all distributions <math>\mu_j</math> are [[Gaussian distribution on a locally compact Abelian group|Gaussian]].

The proof of the theorem relies on group  analogues of [[Cramér's decomposition theorem]]  and the Marcinkiewicz theorem.
